title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
hook: a sinful woman washes his feet with tears at a dinner she wasn't invited to

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the gate of Naim, Jesus saw a grieving widow before anyone asked. Your line was weep not. A new week starts.

A dinner party in a nice house. The host is a Pharisee named Simon, who has asked the new teacher everyone is talking about to eat with him. The guests aren't on chairs; they recline on couches, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them. And someone comes in who was never asked: a woman of the city, known as a sinner, carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. She goes straight to the teacher's feet.
screen: `A DINNER AT SIMON'S HOUSE.` → `GUESTS RECLINING, FEET BEHIND.` → `AN UNINVITED WOMAN WITH A JAR.`

segments.voice: She stands behind him and starts to cry. Her tears fall on his feet, so she wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out the ointment. Simon thinks: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what sort of woman is touching him. Jesus answers the thought with a story. Two men owe a lender money, one five hundred pence, one fifty. Neither can pay, so he forgives them both. Which will love him more? Simon answers carefully: I suppose the one forgiven more. Right, says Jesus. Then he turns toward the woman but keeps talking to Simon. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. Then the line: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loveth less." To her he says: "Thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace." Simon isn't the villain here. He invited Jesus, listened, and answered honestly. The story is about two kinds of guests, and it asks which one we are. Luke never names the woman. For many centuries in the Western Church, following a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was identified with Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar today no longer joins them, and the Gospel itself never says. What Luke does say is that she loved much, and that Jesus sent her away forgiven, in peace.
screen: `TEARS, HAIR, KISSES, OINTMENT.` · `TWO DEBTORS, BOTH FORGIVEN.` · `NO WATER, NO KISS, NO OIL.` · `GO IN PEACE.` · then, large: `SHE HATH LOVED MUCH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been forgiven, by God if you pray, or by a friend, a parent, a partner who let something go, and remember how it felt when they didn't hold it over you. Then think of one person you've been loving carefully, in measured amounts, keeping track, and picture giving them one thing without counting: a kindness, an apology, an hour. If you pray, thank God for what you've been forgiven.
Alabaster. The jar of ointment the unnamed woman poured on Jesus' feet at Simon's dinner, her tears showing how much she knew she'd been forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: go in peace. She was forgiven much, and she loved much. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 456 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMEN WHO FUNDED HIM.`

howItsDone: Catholics connect this story with the sacrament of Penance, where sins are forgiven and the priest sends the penitent away in peace, and some pray with it as an examination of how much they have been forgiven.

fork.setup: you're the host. an uninvited woman with a bad reputation is weeping on your guest's feet. what do you think?
options: if he were a prophet, he'd know what she is.
she's showing the welcome I forgot to give.
someone should ask her to leave.
fork.reveal: Simon thinks the first. Jesus answers with a story, then shows him the second was true: no water, no kiss, no oil from the host.

original.note: Greek: she loved much. The verb is the agape word, love that gives.

trapdoor: what you thought: this is the story of Mary Magdalene washing Jesus' feet.
what it means: an unnamed woman, known as a sinner, shows great love because she knows how much she has been forgiven.
what a scholar hears: Gregory the Great joined her to Mary Magdalene in his Homily 33 on the Gospels; the reformed Roman calendar no longer does.

chat.says: Why did Jesus defend the woman who crashed Simon's dinner?
options: She'd been forgiven much, so she loved much; her tears and ointment showed it.
Simon had forgotten to invite her, and Jesus wanted to correct his manners.
She paid for the dinner, so Jesus said she had a right to be there.
chat.meaning: Jesus told of two forgiven debtors: whoever is forgiven more loves more. Her tears, kisses and ointment showed great love, and he sent her away in peace.

alabaster.meaning: a soft stone carved into jars for ointment

Pharisee.meaning: a member of a Jewish group devoted to keeping the law

Gregory the Great.meaning: a pope whose sermon linked this woman with Mary Magdalene
